About: the light curve of an eclipsing binary of two uniformly bright stars seen edge on

About this simulation

On screen
Top: the two stars on a dark sky, to scale in solar radii, in the frame of the larger star; each disc is coloured like a blackbody at its temperature and drawn brighter the hotter it is, with the Sun's disc to the same scale in the corner. After an eclipse, dashed outlines mark the smaller star at the four contacts ta, tb, tc, td. Bottom: the total brightness F/F0 against time from mid-eclipse, −4 to +4 h, the eclipse with the smaller star in front in one colour and the one with it behind in another.
Controls
The radii Rs (0.5 to 1.5 R⊙) and Rl (2 to 4 R⊙) and the temperatures Ts and Tl (4000 to 10 000 K). Changing any of them returns the clock to 6 h before mid-eclipse, clears the traces and pauses. Play runs one 3-day orbit in about a minute (1.2 h per second).
Measured
a = 20 R⊙ and P = 3.00 days are fixed, so v = 2πa/P = 337 km/s. F/F0 is the total flux over the flux outside eclipse, from the lens-shaped overlap of two uniform discs; a depth is 1 − F/F0 on the floor of an eclipse; in the Guided Inquiry it appears only once that floor has been traced, while Free Exploration shows every depth and timing from the start. The Readouts panel groups the flux, the two depths and the contact timings.
Simplifications
Both discs are uniformly bright (no limb darkening), so each eclipse has a flat floor; the orbit is circular and exactly edge on; and the brightness is the total (bolometric) light, σT4 per unit area. Real light curves have rounded floors, and through a filter the ratio of the surface brightnesses is not exactly (Ts/Tl)4. The contact timings use the circular orbit, so tb − ta over tc − ta is close to, not exactly, Rs/Rl.

Guided Inquiry

1 · Two stars at one temperature

Set Rs = 1.5 solar radii, Rl = 2.5 solar radii and both temperatures to 6000 K. Before pressing play, predict how the two eclipses compare. Then press play and watch one full orbit.

2 · A cooler smaller star

Keep the radii of question 1 and set Ts = 5000 K and Tl = 8000 K. Before pressing play, predict which eclipse is now the deeper. Then press play and compare the two depths in the readouts.

3 · Which eclipse is the primary?

Keep the radii and swap the temperatures, so that Ts = 8000 K and Tl = 5000 K. Before pressing play, predict which rule tells you in every case which eclipse is the deeper, the primary minimum. Then press play and check the rule against the readouts.

4 · Half the temperature

Keep the radii and set Ts = 4000 K and Tl = 8000 K, so that the smaller star has half the temperature of the larger. Before pressing play, predict the depth of the shallower eclipse as a fraction of the depth of the deeper one. Then press play and divide the two depths in the readouts.

5 · Timing the contacts

Set Rs = 1.0 solar radii, Rl = 3.0 solar radii, Ts = 5000 K and Tl = 8000 K. Before pressing play, predict how the time tb − ta for the brightness to slope down compares with the time tc − ta from first contact to the end of the flat floor. Then press play and read both intervals.

6 · A bigger smaller star

Keep the settings of question 5 and raise Rs to 1.5 solar radii. Before pressing play, predict what happens to the depth of the shallower eclipse as a fraction of the depth of the deeper one. Then press play and compare the ratio of the depths with the one you found in question 5.

7 · Summary: reading the two eclipses

In both eclipses the hidden area is the smaller star's disc, πRs2, so the ratio of the two depths is the ratio of the surface brightnesses, (Ts/Tl)4. The deeper eclipse, the primary minimum, is the one that hides the hotter surface.

The timings give the sizes: at orbital speed v the slope lasts about 2Rs/v, and first contact to the end of the floor about 2Rl/v.

This model uses uniformly bright discs, an edge-on circular orbit and total (bolometric) light. Real stars are darker towards the limb, so the floor is rounded, and through a filter the brightness ratio is not exactly (Ts/Tl)4.

The Physics

An Eclipsing Binary · what this sim shows, the physics behind it, and every control

01

At a glance

The orbit is seen edge on, so each star passes in front of the other once an orbit and the total light dips twice. This sim traces both dips for two uniform discs and reads off the depths and contact times.

What you'll learn

  • What fixes the depth of an eclipse.
  • How the two eclipses compare, and which one is called the primary minimum.
  • What the four contact times ta to td measure.
The opening arrangement, to scale: Rs = 1.5 R⊙ and Rl = 2.5 R⊙, seen edge on. The arrow shows which way the smaller star moves.

What's on screen

  • Two discs on a dark sky, to scale and coloured by temperature, with the Sun drawn to the same scale in the corner.
  • Blue line: the light curve F/F0 while the smaller star is in front. Orange line: while it is behind. The dashed line is F/F0 = 1.
  • Dashed outlines of the smaller star at ta, tb, tc, td, drawn once an eclipse has been traced.
  • Readouts: flux, two depths, two timings and the orbital speed.
See itPlay the opening arrangement. Watch for: the smaller star sliding across the larger disc while the blue curve dips and recovers.

03

Both eclipses hide the same area, so equal temperatures give equal depths

With the smaller star in front, its disc covers an area πRs² of the larger star. With it behind, the larger star covers the whole of the smaller disc, the same area πRs². Each eclipse removes that area times the light each unit of the hidden star's surface gives (notes, eq. 2.28).

The same area πRs² is hidden in both eclipses, here for Rs = 1.5 and Rl = 2.5 R⊙.

The depth is measured as a fraction of the light outside eclipse, F0. If both stars have the same temperature, a unit of area gives the same light from either, so the two depths are equal. On the flat floor each is:

depth = Rs2Rs2 + Rl2
Equal temperatures. For Rs = 1.5 and Rl = 2.5 R⊙ this is 2.25/8.5 = 0.2647.
Key idea. Size enters only through the area hidden, which is the same for both eclipses. Any difference in depth must come from the temperatures.
See itPlay both eclipses with both stars at 6000 K. Watch for: the blue and orange curves bottoming out at the same level, and both depth readouts at 0.2647.
04

Depth is set by surface brightness, so the depths are in the ratio (Ts/Tl)4

A unit of a star's disc gives a flux proportional to σSBT⁴. The two fluxes lost are therefore (eq. 2.28, with d the distance to the pair):

ΔFfront = Rs2d2 σSB Tl4,   ΔFbehind = Rs2d2 σSB Ts4
ΔFbehindΔFfront = (TsTl)4
Equations (2.28) and (2.29): Rs cancels in the ratio.
Rs = 1.5 and Rl = 2.5 R⊙, Ts = 5000 K and Tl = 8000 K. Depths 0.3413 and 0.0521; their ratio is (5/8)4 = 0.153.

The deeper eclipse, the primary minimum, hides the hotter star. If the smaller star is the hotter one (Ts = 8000 K, Tl = 5000 K) the depths swap: 0.1072 in front and 0.7023 behind. Changing Rs moves both depths together and leaves their ratio alone.

Ts Tl

These sliders move the sim too. The radii are the sim's current ones.

See itPlay the pair with Ts = 5000 K and Tl = 8000 K. Watch for: the blue curve falling to F/F0 = 0.659 (depth 0.3413) and the orange one only to 0.948 (depth 0.0521).
See itNow swap the temperatures: Ts = 8000 K, Tl = 5000 K. Watch for: the orange curve, smaller star behind, now the deeper: 0.7023 against 0.1072.
See itReturn to 5000 K and 8000 K and shrink Rs to 0.5 R⊙. Watch for: both depths collapsing to 0.0398 and 0.0061, with 0.0061/0.0398 = 0.153 as before.
05

Contact times give the radii, because the smaller star moves at a known speed

Near an eclipse the stars move across the line of sight at the relative speed v = 2πa/Porb. The smaller star first touches the larger at ta, lies wholly inside it at tb, reaches the far edge at tc and leaves at td.

The smaller star at its four contacts, Rs = 1 and Rl = 3 R⊙. From ta to tb it moves through its own diameter; from ta to tc its leading edge crosses the larger diameter.
Rs = v2(tb − ta),   Rl = v2(tc − ta)
Equation (2.27).

Here v = 337 km/s whatever the radii, because a and P are fixed. For Rs = 1 and Rl = 3 R⊙ the sim reads tb − ta = 1.16 h and tc − ta = 3.46 h, a ratio of 0.336, close to Rs/Rl = 1/3. The sim follows the circular orbit, so (2.27) is close rather than exact.

Key idea. Timing gives the radii, once v is known. Depth gives the temperature ratio, and says nothing about size.
See itPlay Rs = 1 R⊙ and Rl = 3 R⊙. Watch for: dashed outlines of the smaller star at ta to td once the eclipse ends, and the timings 1.16 h and 3.46 h.
06

Where it matters: radii, temperatures and masses from one system

  • Radii. In a double-lined eclipsing binary, v = K1 + K2 when sin i = 1, so the contact times give both radii.
  • Temperatures and luminosities. The depths give Ts/Tl; one temperature from the star's colour fixes the other, and L = 4πR²σSBT⁴ follows without knowing the distance.
  • Masses. The same system gives M1 and M2 from the spectroscopic orbit, and spectra taken during the eclipses show which star is hidden at each minimum.
Go deeper: what this sim leaves out

Both discs are uniformly bright and the orbit is exactly edge on, so every floor is flat. Real discs are darker at the edge, and an orbit not quite edge on rounds the floor. In a single photometric band the depth ratio is the ratio of the fluxes a unit area emits in that band, not exactly (Ts/Tl)⁴.

07

Summary

In one line. The light curve of an eclipsing binary records how much light each eclipse removes and how long each contact takes.
  • Both eclipses hide the area πRs², so they differ only through surface brightness.
  • ΔFbehind/ΔFfront = (Ts/Tl)⁴, and the deeper eclipse hides the hotter star.
  • Rs = (v/2)(tb − ta) and Rl = (v/2)(tc − ta), with v = 2πa/Porb.

Common mix-ups

  • "The deeper eclipse is the one with the larger star in front." The temperature decides. At Ts = 8000 K and Tl = 5000 K the deeper eclipse, 0.7023, is the smaller star passing behind.
  • "A bigger smaller star changes the ratio of the depths." It deepens both eclipses together. At 5000 K and 8000 K it raises both, 0.0398 to 0.3413 and 0.0061 to 0.0521, and the ratio stays 0.153.

Things to try on your own

  • Set Ts = Tl and change Rl from 2 to 4 R⊙. Check each reading against Rs²/(Rs² + Rl²).
  • Set Rs = 0.5 and Rl = 4 R⊙, and recover both radii from the two timings and v = 1.745 R⊙/h.
